The intersection keeps just the shared edges A–B and B–D; A–C and C–D are dashed, and node C, left with no edges, is dropped too." width="100%"} Returns a new graph containing only edges that exist in both graphs. Nodes are included only if they are endpoints of common edges. Edges are matched by their endpoint node IDs: an edge counts as shared when both graphs connect the same pair of IDs (in the same direction, for directed graphs). Weights and attributes play no part in the matching, so an edge with weight `1.0` in one graph and `3.0` in the other is still shared. Intersection answers "which connections are present everywhere?", which is useful for: - finding the stable core of a network observed at several points in time - keeping only interactions confirmed by two independent data sources or experiments - comparing two inferred networks (e.g., from different methods) for agreement Because nodes are matched by ID, both graphs must use the same numbering for the same entities. Nodes that are not part of any shared edge are dropped, even if both graphs contain them. Edges keep this graph's IDs. Neither input graph is modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to intersect with. It must have the same directedness as this graph. Only its edge set (by endpoint IDs) decides which edges survive; for surviving edges and nodes, its labels, attributes, and weights are used only where this graph has no value of its own. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph containing edges present in both graphs, plus their endpoints. It is weighted if either input is weighted. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Intersection keeps only edges present in both graphs and drops any node that would end up isolated as a result, matching the algebraic identity $E(G_1 \cap G_2) = E_1 \cap E_2$ followed by node pruning. Both operands must share the same directedness. Where both graphs carry a weight, label, or attribute for the same edge or node, the calling graph's value wins and the other graph fills in only what the calling graph lacks, which is worth knowing when weights differ. A common use is identifying the stable core of a network observed at multiple time points. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Only the edges present in both graphs survive -- here, both graphs share edges `1-2` and `2-3`, but the triangle's closing edge and the square's extra edges don't overlap: ::: {#8eed56e3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Triangle g1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): g1.add_node() g1.add_edge(1, 2) g1.add_edge(2, 3) g1.add_edge(3, 1) # Square with diagonal g2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 5): g2.add_node() g2.add_edge(1, 2) g2.add_edge(2, 3) g2.add_edge(3, 4) g2.add_edge(4, 1) common = g1.intersection(g2) common.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Node `4` exists only in the square and touches no shared edge, so it is not part of the intersection: ::: {#24c94b26 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} sorted(common.get_node_ids()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [1, 2, 3] ``` ::: ::: This is useful for finding stable connections that exist at multiple time points or in multiple network versions. Two yearly snapshots of a friendship network, built with the same people in the same order (so they get the same IDs), share three friendships: ::: {#2f2dc143 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def snapshot(friendships): g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes(["Ann", "Bob", "Cat", "Dan", "Eve"]) g.add_edges(friendships) return g year1 = snapshot([("Ann", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Cat"), ("Cat", "Dan"), ("Dan", "Eve")]) year2 = snapshot([("Ann", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Cat"), ("Ann", "Cat"), ("Dan", "Eve")]) year1.intersection(year2).get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['Ann--Bob', 'Bob--Cat', 'Dan--Eve'] ``` ::: ::: In directed graphs direction matters: `A -> B` and `B -> A` are different edges, so these two graphs have nothing in common: ::: {#1993618c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} d1 = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_node(label="A").add_node(label="B").add_edge("A", "B") d2 = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_node(label="A").add_node(label="B").add_edge("B", "A") d1.intersection(d2).count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 0 ``` ::: :::
